title: Neighbors of other faiths
tomorrow: the junior from the bus stop goes down hurt. does Simran bring water?

cards: It's Mrs. Haddad from across the hall, holding a round loaf wrapped in a dish towel. She tears it at the table, says bismillah under her breath, and asks Arjan's mom, kindly, whether they're Muslim too.
Simran feels a whole lecture loading: the turban, the Gurus, how people mix Sikhs up with everyone. She opens her mouth. And then she remembers something odd she read this week.
A hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib opens, in paraphrase, with this: first, Allah created the light. Allah. In Sikh scripture.

teach.b: The hymn is by Kabir, on Ang 1349, and it keeps going. In paraphrase: first, Allah created the light; all people are made by the Creator's power.

teach.h: FROM ONE LIGHT, THE WHOLE WORLD.
teach.b: From one light the whole world welled up. So who is good, and who is bad? Here's the puzzle solved.
Kabir uses the name his Muslim neighbors used, and he uses it to say the one light made everyone at that table.
The Guru Granth Sahib calls the One by many names, Ram, Hari, Allah, Waheguru, and it gathers voices from outside the Sikh fold too.

teach.h: SHEIKH FARID'S HYMNS IN THE GRANTH.
teach.b: That's the detail worth telling a friend tonight: the Sikh scripture holds the hymns of Sheikh Farid, a Muslim Sufi, sung in gurdwaras alongside the Gurus' own.
So the scripture's first move with a neighbor isn't a comparison chart. It's recognition: same light, same Maker's hand. That doesn't erase what's different.
Sikhs and Muslims pray differently, keep different practices, and hold different scriptures, and an honest friendship can talk about all of it when someone asks.
But that's the second conversation, not the first. Simran closes the lecture tab in her head. She says: no, we're Sikh.
Thank you for the bread. Do you take your chai sweet? Mrs.

how: Sikhs sing the hymns of Kabir and Sheikh Farid alongside the Gurus' hymns, and gurdwaras welcome neighbors of every faith or none to sit in the langar.

games.q: what does “neighbors of other faiths” mean?
o: joining in another faith's worship to show you respect it
friendship with people of other paths, before any comparing
a rule to avoid talking about religion with people at work

games.q: one light, many names — tap the pairs.
p: a Muslim Sufi whose hymns are in the Granth

s: being a good neighbor means first explaining how your faiths differ
the scripture's first move is recognition, the one light; differences are the second conversation.
a hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib opens with Allah creating the light
Kabir, Ang 1349, in paraphrase: first, Allah created the light.
the Guru Granth Sahib holds hymns by a Muslim Sufi, Sheikh Farid
his hymns are sung in gurdwaras alongside the Gurus' own.

games.q: a friend's family invites you to break the fast with them during Ramadan. you don't fast. going by today, what fits best?
o: go, eat when they eat, and ask them what the evening means to them.
politely say no, since it's their faith's meal and not yours.
go, and bring a short talk on how fasting works in your own faith.
games.why: friendship first: show up and recognize the light. honest differences can come later, when someone asks.

practice: Bring to mind a neighbor or coworker whose faith isn't yours, or who has none. Choose one ordinary kindness that has nothing to do with religion: returning a dish, asking about their weekend, sharing something you cooked.
Hold their face in mind for a few breaths, and settle on when you'll do it.

wordCard.voice: Neighbors of other faiths. Friendship that starts with the one light, and leaves comparing for later, if anyone asks.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: noor, light. Kabir on Ang 1349: from one light the whole world welled up.

carryVoice: Here's the line: friendship first, the way Kabir started with one light. Bread, chai, and day 1731, very sweet.
